query: For high-entropy alloys intended for structural applications, what testable methodological hypothesis could enable improved combinations of strength, ductility, Young’s modulus, and fracture resistance? Explain why it should work, what measurable improvement is expected relative to the state of the art, the conditions under which it should or should not hold, the prior evidence supporting it, and an experimental result that would decisively falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: A controlled thermo‐mechanical treatment (TMT) consisting of homogenization, severe plastic deformation, and rapid annealing will generate a stable, dual‐phase microstructure with refined grains and uniformly dispersed nanoscale precipitates in HEAs, thereby enabling simultaneous improvements in strength, ductility, Young’s modulus, and fracture resistance.
generation.material_initial_state: An as‐cast, arc‐melted high‐entropy alloy (typically with a single-phase or coarse dual-phase microstructure with grain sizes on the order of several hundred microns).
generation.intervention: Apply a sequential processing route: first homogenize the as‐cast HEA (e.g., at ~1000 °C for 2 h under inert conditions) to reduce chemical inhomogeneities, then subject the material to severe plastic deformation (such as 50% hot rolling) to refine the microstructure followed by rapid annealing at temperatures in the range of 800–900 °C for a short duration (e.g., 30–60 s) to stabilize a dual-phase structure.
generation.conditions: The method should be executed under an inert atmosphere to avoid oxidation, and the process window must be optimized for alloys with moderate alloying element contrasts. The hypothesis is expected to hold when the HEA composition is not overly skewed toward brittle phase formation and when processing parameters are tightly controlled; excessive annealing or inappropriate deformation may lead to unwanted grain growth or phase instability.
generation.structural_mediator: A refined, dual-phase microstructure featuring a fine grain size and uniformly distributed nanoscale precipitates that act as obstacles to dislocation motion.
generation.mechanism: Severe plastic deformation increases dislocation density and refines grains (via the Hall–Petch effect), while rapid annealing promotes recovery and stabilizes a small-scale dual-phase arrangement. This microstructure simultaneously enhances yield strength (from grain-boundary strengthening), maintains ductility (by avoiding excessive brittleness common in single highly-stiff phases), and increases Young’s modulus and fracture resistance (through the presence of stable, reinforcing precipitates).
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to the as‐cast state, the TMT-processed HEA is predicted to show an improvement on the order of approximately 10–20% in yield strength and fracture resistance, while either maintaining or modestly increasing ductility and Young’s modulus.
generation.baseline: Performance metrics of standard as‐cast, arc‐melted HEAs with coarse grains (e.g., grain sizes of 400–500 μm) and less optimal phase distributions.
generation.boundary: The method’s benefits may not manifest in HEA compositions with a high volume fraction of intrinsically brittle phases or in cases where the processing parameters (deformation amount, annealing temperature/duration) are not within the optimal window. Unintended grain growth or phase degradation could negate the improvements.
generation.uncertainty: The precise quantitative improvements and the optimal TMT parameters will depend on the specific HEA composition. Variability in alloy stability and phase evolution during processing introduces some uncertainty about the magnitude and consistency of the performance gains.

falsification_experiment.design: Divide a batch of as‐cast HEA samples into two groups. Subject one group to the proposed TMT route (homogenization, 50% hot rolling, rapid annealing at 800–900 °C for 30–60 s) while keeping the other group as a control (standard as‐cast condition). Conduct microstructural characterization (using SEM/TEM to assess grain size and phase distribution) and mechanical testing (tensile testing for yield strength and ductility, three-point bending for Young’s modulus, and fracture toughness tests).
measurements: Grain size and phase distribution via SEM/TEM
Yield strength, ultimate tensile strength, and uniform elongation from tensile tests
Young’s modulus from three-point bending or ultrasonic measurements
Fracture toughness and/or fracture resistance from standardized impact or crack propagation tests
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the TMT-processed samples do not show at least a 10–20% improvement in the key mechanical properties (yield strength, ductility, Young’s modulus, fracture resistance) compared to the control samples, or if adverse microstructural changes (such as significant grain growth or phase instability) are observed, the hypothesis will be considered falsified.

cited_evidence.text: The following design criteria for the selection of best HEA compositions were considered: (1) high energetical stability, (2) lightweight, (3) large elastic modulus, (4) large specific stiffness, and (5) high Pugh’s ratio (which indicates the alloy ductility vs. its brittleness). The five topmost compositions were selected according to the design criteria for each of the three HEA families. The present work, for the first time, employed HT and HF first-principles-based methods to design lightweight HEAs. It is widely acknowledged that designing and fabricating lightweight HEAs with stable structures and superior mechanical properties remains a challenge. Our study reveals that HEAs with the topmost compositions exhibit a negative formation energy, low mass density and high specific Young’s modulus, but a low Pugh’s ratio. These results indicate that the designed lightweight HEAs can be energetically more stable, lighter, and stiffer compared to existing Al alloys. However, they may exhibit a low ductility. These findings will provide valuable insights and guidance for experimental development and fabrication of lightweight HEAs with desirable properties.

In the present study we focus on development of ceramic-reinforced HEA composites with a fcc matrix as part of a wider search of materials with improved combinations of strength and ductility. The CoCrFeNi system, as one of the most widely studied fcc HEAs, was selected as the matrix material for the study. For the ceramic phase WC is chosen, due to is relatively good toughness and its widespread use as a high density ceramic material in demanding applications. Using these starting materials CoCrFeNi-WC composites were prepared by an arc melting process. The evolution of microstructure and crystal structure were studied as a function of WC weight fraction, together with an investigation of the mechanical properties of the HEA-ceramic composites.

cited_evidence.kind: web:3.2. Performance of the Zr7 MEA after TMT Processing
cited_evidence.text: Before they underwent TMT processing, the as-cast Zr7 MEA ingots were homogenized at 1000 °C for 2 h to eliminate composition inhomogeneity and dendritic microstructures. Figure 2; Figure 4 clearly reveal that the dendrites were effectively eliminated after homogenization and that the grain grew apparently from 83 to 485 μm. The homogenized Zr7 MEA ingots were further processed through TMT and rapid annealing; the samples underwent CR70 and HR50CR70 rolling processing, and they were then rapidly annealed for 30, 40, 50, and 60 s at a heating rate of 15 K/s to reach the temperatures of 742 °C, 812 °C, 854 °C, and 881 °C, respectively. Figure 4e suggests that the grain size of the Zr7 MEA after hot rolling was effectively reduced from 485 to 142 μm. The XRD results reveal that all the samples retained their single BCC structure irrespective of the applied processing route (Figure 5), indicating that the Zr7 MEA exhibits strong solid solution phase stability at high temperatures.
